knowledge_point.title: Transforming First-Order Linear ODEs Using Integrating Factors

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y = y(x)$:
$\frac{dy}{dx}-\left(6 x\right)\cdot y=8 x e^{3 x^{2}}$
Write the equation in the form $\frac{d}{dx}(yI(x)) = I(x)Q(x)$, where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=- 6 x$ and $Q(x)=8 x e^{3 x^{2}}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & =e^{\int \left(- 6 x\right)\,dx} \\  & =e^{- 3 x^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)=e^{- 3 x^{2}}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left(e^{- 3 x^{2}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{dy}{dx}-\left(6 x\right)\cdot y\right) & =\left(e^{- 3 x^{2}}\right)\cdot \left(8 x e^{3 x^{2}}\right) \\ \left(e^{- 3 x^{2}}\right)\cdot \frac{dy}{dx}-\left(6 x\right)\cdot \left(e^{- 3 x^{2}}\right)\cdot y & =\left(e^{- 3 x^{2}}\right)\cdot \left(8 x e^{3 x^{2}}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}\left(y\cdot \left(e^{- 3 x^{2}}\right)\right) & =\left(e^{- 3 x^{2}}\right)\cdot \left(8 x e^{3 x^{2}}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y=y(x):$

$$
\left(x^{2}\right)\cdot \frac{dy}{dx}-\left(4 x\right)\cdot y=x^{2} \cos{\left(4 x \right)},\,x>0
$$

Write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yI(x))=I(x)Q(x),$ where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we write the equation in standard form. This gives

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}-\left(\frac{4}{x}\right)\cdot y=\cos{\left(4 x \right)}.
$$

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=- \frac{4}{x}$ and $Q(x)=\cos{\left(4 x \right)}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & =e^{\int \left(- \frac{4}{x}\right)\,dx} \\  & =e^{- 4 \ln{\left(x \right)}} \\  & =e^{\ln \left(\frac{1}{x^{4}}\right)} \\  & =\frac{1}{x^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)=\frac{1}{x^{4}}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left(\frac{1}{x^{4}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{dy}{dx}-\left(\frac{4}{x}\right)\cdot y\right) & =\left(\frac{1}{x^{4}}\right)\cdot \left(\cos{\left(4 x \right)}\right) \\ \left(\frac{1}{x^{4}}\right)\cdot \frac{dy}{dx}-\left(\frac{4}{x}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{1}{x^{4}}\right)\cdot y & =\frac{\cos{\left(4 x \right)}}{x^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x)):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}\left(y\cdot \left(\frac{1}{x^{4}}\right)\right) & =\frac{\cos{\left(4 x \right)}}{x^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y=y(x):$

$$
\left(x\right)\cdot \frac{dy}{dx}-\left(4\right)\cdot y=4
$$

Write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yI(x))=I(x)Q(x),$ where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.

Assume $x>0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we write the equation in standard form. This gives

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}-\left(\frac{4}{x}\right)\cdot y=\frac{4}{x}.
$$

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=- \frac{4}{x}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{4}{x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & =e^{\int \left(- \frac{4}{x}\right)\,dx} \\  & =e^{- 4 \ln{\left(x \right)}} \\  & =e^{\ln \left(\frac{1}{x^{4}}\right)} \\  & =\frac{1}{x^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)=\frac{1}{x^{4}}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left(\frac{1}{x^{4}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{dy}{dx}-\left(\frac{4}{x}\right)\cdot y\right) & =\left(\frac{1}{x^{4}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{4}{x}\right) \\ \left(\frac{1}{x^{4}}\right)\cdot \frac{dy}{dx}-\left(\frac{4}{x}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{1}{x^{4}}\right)\cdot y & =\left(\frac{1}{x^{4}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{4}{x}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x)):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}\left(y\cdot \left(\frac{1}{x^{4}}\right)\right) & =\left(\frac{1}{x^{4}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{4}{x}\right)\end{aligned}
$$
